$comment: The demo topology: what `make demo` starts, in what order, and how it knows each one is up.
Order matters. The collector comes first because every role emits into it, and a role that
starts before it is listening loses whatever it emits in the meantime — there is no retry,
on purpose, because an event log that pushed back on the roles would be the coupling ADR
0003 forbids. The frontend comes last because it proxies to the collector and there is
nothing to look at until the roles are running.
The form each `health` below is written in matches what that process binds, and the
correspondence is the thing to keep. collector and agent bind the literal 127.0.0.1 and
are probed by literal. The four roles bind a bare `:port`, which is the dual-stack wildcard, so
localhost reaches them whichever family the resolver answers with. The frontend was the one
exception, and issue #267 is what that cost: the probe here is a literal, but Vite's default
`server.host` is the *name* localhost, and Node >= 17 resolves names without reordering to put
IPv4 first — so on a machine answering ::1 first the dev server bound [::1] alone, nothing
answered on 127.0.0.1, and `make demo` called the frontend failed for thirty seconds while the
page it was serving worked in a browser. A browser survives what a health check cannot because a
name carries a list of addresses and a client that fails on the first tries the next; an IP
literal has no list and no fallback. frontend/src/topology.test.ts now fails if this file and
vite.config.ts disagree about where the dev server listens.
The agent comes after the roles and before the frontend. Every role above it has either
answered its health check or been reported as a stub by then, so the console it serves is
backed by a stack that is up before a browser can reach it. **Nothing is emitted before the
browser is there** since issue #313, which is what changed about this paragraph: the ring and
the SSE replay used to be what let a browser attaching afterwards see a transaction that had
already happened, and now they are what lets a *second* tab, or a reconnect, see one this one
started. Same mechanism, and it stopped being load-bearing for the first page load.
**Nothing here buys anything, and issue #313 is where that was decided.** This manifest used
to start two agents: one given a bare `-watch`, which fell back to cmd/agent's defaultPrompt
and had the flight authorised and being watched before the port was even bound, and one given
`-buy`, which ran a complete Human Present purchase of the same flight. So `make demo` opened
on two transactions nobody had asked for, and the one screen that exists to show a purchase
being authorised opened with a purchase nobody had authorised in front of them. A viewer could
not tell what they had done from what the stack had done for them, which is the first thing a
demonstration has to make obvious.
Both are gone and the agent below starts nothing. What replaced the boot watch is the console
it already served: a browser posts to POST /watches, so the first transaction on screen is one
somebody made. What replaced agent-buy is nothing, and that cost is real and stated rather than
hidden — the Human Present flow is no longer exercised by `make demo`, so a regression in it
now shows up in CI and in `cmd/agent -buy` from a terminal, and no longer in front of whoever
was about to take a screenshot. It was traded for an empty screen deliberately.
One agent, so it is named `agent`. **Each entry is named for what distinguishes it**, and while
there were two agents what distinguished them was the flag each ran — `agent-watch` against
`agent-buy`. With `-watch` gone and no sibling to tell it apart from, a name stating a flag this
entry does not pass would have been the drift that rule exists to prevent. cmd/agent still takes -buy and -watch, and
still refuses -buy beside -addr at parse time (issue #257, flagsAgree in
backend/cmd/agent/main.go); what changed is which of those flags this file reaches for, which
is now neither.
**What the empty start costs is the guarantee that a verifier ever refuses anything**, and it
is worth knowing before running this. The watch attempts on every step change and never
compares money to the cap — the merchant's verifier is what refuses — so which beats a run
shows depends on where the cycling schedule is when the watch takes its baseline. Against the
flight's three prices a baseline of $240 gives the designed pair, $189 gives two refusals
before the buy, and $210 gives a single clean purchase and no refusal at all: two phases of
three. Against a two-price offer where one price clears the cap and the other does
not — the bicycle, and every scripted sentence there is — it is one of two. Against an offer
whose prices are all inside the cap it is none: nothing is ever refused, which is what
`"found": "always"` marks in deploy/catalogue.json and what most of that file is. The boot watch used to fix that by taking
its baseline 0.45 seconds after the merchant started, which is what the start order used to be
arranged for — the order below no longer carries that reason, and a reader looking for it in
the list will not find one. A person clicking Buy lands wherever the lap has got to.
That is accepted rather than repaired, and the alternatives are why. Resetting the merchant's
schedule when a watch starts would be a verifier's clock moving because a buyer arrived, which
is backwards. Holding the first price until somebody buys would make the schedule a fixture
rather than a clock. What is left is that the sequence cycles, so a run that showed no refusal
can simply be run again, and POST /demo/advance is there for a presenter who would rather not
wait — the merchant below carries -demo-controls for exactly that.
The agent states -poll where the merchant above it states -step and -step-max, because
those numbers only mean anything together. The watch triggers on the merchant's step
changing, so a poll longer than a step would step over the $210 the verifier is meant to
refuse and go straight from $240 to $189 — beat 5 of the built scenario, the one where a
verifier says no, would simply not happen. Issue #158 made -step and -step-max a range rather
than a fixed duration: each price now holds a random width drawn once from [-step, -step-max]
instead of the same thirty seconds every time. Issue #177 then made the sequence cycle back
to its first price instead of holding the last one forever, so what -step-max actually wires
below is merchant.NewCyclingJitteredSchedule — see the paragraph on the wrap, further down, for
what that changes and does not change about the argument this file makes. What -poll has to
stay under either way is not the pair's average but its floor, -step itself, the shortest a
price can ever hold. One second against a three-to-six-second range is at least three polls a
step even in the worst case, and the whole watched-refused-bought flow now completes in
roughly twelve seconds — two transitions at up to six seconds each — rather than the two and a
half minutes two fixed thirty-second steps used to take. Shortening -step here still has to
bring -poll down with it, on the same terms as before: -poll must stay comfortably below
-step, which a reader can only notice if every number in the pair is in this file.
**-step has a second thing to clear and it is on the frontend, so issue #344 left it here.**
The three lanes put a gap between steps — an attempt emits eleven of them in a burst under a
tenth of a second, and a room cannot follow a flicker. The rule they draw under is that
whatever has arrived is on screen within DRAIN_MS of arriving, which is two seconds in
frontend/src/lanes/pace.ts. **-step must stay above that**, or the next attempt starts before
the last one has finished drawing and the queue never empties. Three against two is the
margin, and it is the reason this range is stated here rather than left to the merchant's
own defaults.
That number was 750 ms *per step* and fixed, which is 8.25 seconds of drawing per attempt
against a step as short as three. The screen built a backlog it could never work off and the
notice that made the pacing honest ('10 steps have arrived and are still being drawn') became
permanent, which is indistinguishable from a stall. Widening this range to 8s-12s was the
first fix and it was the wrong one: it slowed the demonstration down to protect a screen
behaviour nobody wanted. Deleting the pacing was the second, and it made the burst
unreadable. The bound is the third, and it is what makes three seconds enough.
**-step used to have a second number to clear, and issue #313 retired it.** The merchant's
schedule starts when the merchant starts — merchant.NewDemoService reads it off the clock at
construction — and the boot watch was further down this list, so the price it took as its
baseline was whatever was in force by the time the runner reached it. A baseline already past
the first boundary was already the $210, and beat 5 was gone as silently as a slow poll would
have lost it: one attempt, bought at $189, no error anywhere. Putting the watching agent above
the buying one, and a measured 0.45 seconds of margin against a 3s floor, were what bought that
guarantee, and
TestTheMerchantsFirstPriceOutlastsTheStackComingUp was what held it.
With nothing started at boot there is no such window: the baseline is taken when a person
clicks, wherever the lap has got to. That test went with the guarantee rather than being left
asserting a property of a watch that no longer exists — see pacing_internal_test.go, which
records why. What replaces it is the paragraph above: the refusal is likely rather than
certain, the sequence cycles, and POST /demo/advance is the presenter's way past it.
TestThePollStaysUnderTheShortestPriceHold still pins the -poll paragraph three above this one.
It was edited here rather than left alone — it looked the agent up by the old process name —
but what it asserts did not move: that property never depended on when a watch started, because
whoever starts one, it triggers on the merchant's step changing, so -poll has to clear the
shortest hold a price can ever take.
**And the hold it has to clear is the same on every lap.** Issue #177 made the sequence cycle:
the `-step-max` set below wires `merchant.NewCyclingJitteredSchedule`, whose sequence never
stops — for an offer with more than one price. That qualifier is about the constructor rather
than about anything this manifest starts: a single price has nothing to wrap to, so it builds
the same held-still schedule a one-shot one would, and issue #192 is what that used to cost the
two offers in deploy/catalogue.json that carried one. Every offer that file ships now carries at
least two, so nothing below is held still. A wrap that shortened the hold nearest the seam would
let a slow poll steal back on lap two what it cleared on lap one, and nothing here would notice,
because everything here is reasoned once. `TestACyclingScheduleShortensNoHoldAtTheWrap`, in
`internal/roles/merchant`'s own suite, rules that out analytically rather than by sampling a
run: every hold this schedule ever produces, the wrap included, lies in [-step, -step-max], so
the floor this file measures against is a property of the constructor rather than a fact about
the first lap. It holds identically on lap one and on lap one thousand — which matters more now
than it did, because a person clicking Buy an hour into a run is on a late lap by construction.
The four identifiers the agent can also be given are not restated, for the opposite reason.
They have to agree with cmd/merchant, cmd/credprovider and cmd/mpp, none of which is given one
here either — so both sides are the flag's default today, and a value written here could only
ever drift from the binary it names.
The merchant's `-catalogue` is not restated either, and on that same rule rather than by
oversight. It defaults to `../deploy/catalogue.json`, which resolves from the `backend` working
directory below, so a value here would say what the binary already says. What makes `-step`,
`-step-max` and `-poll` the exception is that they only mean anything together: the group has
to be read as one, which a reader can only do if every number in it is in this file. A path has
no partner.
**`-catalogue-live` is not here either, and that is the same decision `-interpreter auto` got**
— issue #243. The merchant can be told to fetch a public test shop's stock at start-up and sell
it beside the committed file, which is what makes a model-backed interpreter worth having: a
sentence that arrives at sixty-four offers written down in this repository proves nothing a
lookup table could not, and the interpreter only starts doing work when the shelf is one nobody
has seen. `make demo-live` appends it, at the runner, exactly as it appends the interpreter
flag.
The reasoning differs from the interpreter's in one way worth stating, because it is the way
that would justify writing it here and does not. `-interpreter auto` was kept out of this file
because naming it here makes the *opt-in* visible without making the *outcome* deterministic —
GEMINI_API_KEY still decides. `-catalogue-live` has no such ambient input: named here, it would
be perfectly deterministic in the sense that every run would fetch. It stays out because of
what that determinism would be: **`make demo` would reach a network**, the offers on screen
would be whatever a shop had in stock that day, and every committed screenshot's numbers would
stop being attributable. The one target this manifest exists to keep predictable is `make
demo`, and this flag is precisely a way to make it unpredictable.
It also fails differently from the interpreter, and a reader should know before typing the
command. An unset key is an answer, so `auto` falls back to the scripted table and says so; a
shop that will not answer is not an answer, so the merchant **stops** rather than quietly
serving the committed file under a label saying it did not. `make demo-live` therefore needs a
network where `make demo` needs none, and a run of it that fails at the merchant has failed
loudly on purpose.
What a fetched offer can demonstrate is narrower than what the four below can, and the merchant
says so in its own start-up output rather than leaving it to be discovered. A fetched offer
holds the one price the shop quotes, and a Human Not Present watch attempts only on a step
change — so a sentence with a condition in it cannot resolve against one, ever. An instruction
can, which is the distinction issue #198 put behind the interpretation's trigger. The beats
everything else in this file is written about — $240 watched, $210 refused, $189 bought — are
the flight's schedule and are untouched by any of it.
The agent gets `-addr`, which is what turns it into a server: it serves the
console API of #137, so a browser can start a watch and poll where each mandate in it stands.
Since issue #313 that is the only reason this process exists — it authorises nothing of its own
and the flag is what the whole demonstration now hangs from, where it used to be the second of
two things this entry did. The flag defaults to empty meaning do not serve, which is why the
agent-buy that used to sit below carried no -addr and no health check; both are gone with it.
A watch is started *through* this console rather than beside it — nothing starts one
here on its own — so the terminal and the browser are looking at
one run; frontend/vite.config.ts proxies /watches here, which is why the port is stated in both
files and has to move in both.
The agent does not get `-interpreter auto`. Writing it into this file was considered and set
aside: a flag in a reviewed, committed manifest makes the *opt-in* visible, but it does not make
the *outcome* deterministic — whether the agent would then read free text still turns on
whether the shell running `make demo` happens to export GEMINI_API_KEY, so two machines running
the identical command would show two different demonstrations and nothing in this file would say
which. `make demo` is the one target this manifest exists to keep predictable, so the flag stays
out of it and the agent's args below leave -interpreter at cmd/agent's own default, `scripted`
— argued at length in that package's doc, and unconditionally what every process here runs.
`gemini` was never a candidate either, on its own refusal: `-interpreter gemini` with no key
refuses to start at all, which would break `make demo` on every machine that has none, and most
do.
**The opt-in lives in the Makefile instead, as `make demo-live`** — the same nine processes
below, unmodified, with `-interpreter auto` handed to the agent and `-catalogue-live dummyjson`
to the merchant by `cmd/demo`'s own `-append` flag rather than by an edit here — two processes
and two flags since issue #243, which is the paragraph above. That is the shape that cannot
drift the way a second manifest would: there is exactly one topology, this one, and the live
variant differs from it by flags applied at the runner rather than by a second file
enumerating the same nine processes
and going stale against this one the moment either changes without the other. See
backend/cmd/demo/main.go's own doc for -append's syntax and the same argument in fewer words.
A person running `make demo-live` is the deliberate naming interpreterFor's package doc asks for
in place of a silent fallback: a command typed is attributable in a way a shell variable already
exported never is, because typing it is the one thing that cannot happen by accident. It costs
the golden numbers on exactly the machine that typed it — with a key present, the agent reads
free text and answers with whatever the model returns, no longer `interpret.Scenarios()`'s fixed
five — and that is safe for the same reason `-interpreter gemini`'s refusal to fall back exists
in the first place: the console states which mode it is in before the box is touched, and says
neither sentence until GET /examples has actually answered, so a browser that cannot reach this
agent is never told it reads free text on the agent's behalf. Without a key, `make demo-live`
shows exactly what `make demo` does — `auto` builds `interpret.Demo()`, the same value
`-interpreter scripted` returns — so the only machine where this target's output differs from
the plain one is the machine that asked it to.
The merchant runs with `-demo-controls`, so `POST /demo/advance` moves its clock on by
exactly `-step` — the floor of the range, not a random draw of its own; see
merchant.DemoOptions.StepMax. It moves everything that merchant was built to read: the
prices, offer expiry, mandate expiry, challenge freshness, and the window its idempotency
store forgets records after. That is deliberate — the control says time passed rather than
that the price changed — and it is a property of how merchant.NewDemoService wires the
process, not of the endpoint. Off by default everywhere else: an endpoint that moves a
verifier's clock belongs in a demonstration and nowhere near anything real.
Nothing in `make demo` presses this control automatically — the automated flow lets the wall
clock carry the schedule at its own -step/-step-max cadence, which is what makes the twelve
second target true without anybody clicking anything. The control is for a presenter skipping
ahead by hand, and skipping ahead under a jittered schedule is imprecise in one specific way:
since a step's own random width can land anywhere up to `-step-max`, one press of exactly
`-step` is not guaranteed to cross it, and an occasional second press may be needed. That is
accepted rather than solved — solving it would mean the control asking the schedule for its
own next boundary instead of moving by a fixed duration, which is a bigger change than a
presenter's convenience needs.
It needs an `Idempotency-Key`, like every unsafe method here, and a repeat under the same key
replays the first answer instead of advancing again — which is what makes a double-clicked
button harmless and what makes two steps need two keys.
`implemented: false` marks a binary that is still a stub. The runner starts it anyway and
expects it to exit — which is how a stale flag becomes visible rather than silently wrong.
Flip it in the pull request that implements the role.

processes.name: collector
processes.summary: gathers protocol events and streams them to the frontend over SSE
processes.note: Demo infrastructure. Not an AP2 role and not a TAP identity party — see ADR 0003.

processes.name: surface
processes.summary: Trusted Surface — shows the interpretation and takes the user's signature

processes.name: merchant
processes.summary: Merchant — prices the route and verifies the Checkout Mandate
processes.note: Advance the schedule instead of waiting it out — a fresh key per step, since a repeat replays: curl -X POST -H 'Idempotency-Key: step-1' http://localhost:8081/demo/advance

processes.name: credprovider
processes.summary: Credential Provider — issues a payment credential scoped to one checkout

processes.name: mpp
processes.summary: Merchant Payment Processor — verifies the Payment Mandate

processes.name: registry
processes.summary: local agent registry — resolves an agent's key reference

processes.name: proxy
processes.summary: verifying proxy at the merchant edge — checks RFC 9421 signatures

processes.name: agent
processes.summary: Shopping Agent — serves the console a browser starts a purchase from, and runs whatever it is asked to watch
processes.note: It starts nothing of its own: the screen is empty until somebody buys something. A watch is started from the browser, or by hand — curl -X POST -H 'Idempotency-Key: one-click' -d '{"prompt":"buy a flight to Palma when it drops below $200, this summer"}' http://127.0.0.1:8086/watches — and GET http://127.0.0.1:8086/watches lists every one. Human Not Present, beats 4 to 6 against the flight: $240.00 watched, $210.00 refused with a signed receipt, $189.00 bought; which of those beats a given run sees depends on where the merchant's cycling schedule is when the watch takes its baseline, and POST /demo/advance is how a presenter moves it on. GET http://127.0.0.1:8086/watches/{id}/attempts/1/presented is the four chains that attempt presented, each beside the verifier it was addressed to — it is what #21's Mandate Inspector reads, and the chains are deliberately not on the polled view

processes.name: frontend
processes.summary: two screens: Buying, where a purchase is proposed and signed for, and The protocol, which explains what that produced
